Right: those two edges are gone, shown dashed, while all six nodes and the other five edges stay in place." width="100%"} Removes edges in the current selection from the graph. Node connectivity may be affected, but nodes themselves remain in the graph. Updates selection state automatically. Like the other `_ws` ("with selection") methods, this acts on the current edge selection instead of taking arguments. Build the selection with `select_edges()` (a predicate on edge objects), `select_edges_by_id()`, `select_edges_by_node()` or an edge traversal such as `trav_out_edge()`, then delete everything selected in one call. Common uses include: - pruning weak connections below a weight threshold - removing edges of a particular `rel` type - cutting the edges around a set of nodes while keeping the nodes themselves The deleted edges are removed from the edge selection (which ends up empty), and an empty selection makes the call a no-op. Removing edges can disconnect the graph or leave isolated nodes behind. The graph is modified in place and, when at least one edge is removed, the deletion is recorded as a single step in the step log (see `steps`). To delete selected nodes together with their edges, use `delete_nodes_ws()`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Self for method chaining. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} This operates on the current edge selection. Deleting the two middle edges of a five-node path leaves every node in place, since removing edges never removes nodes. Only the first and last edges of the path remain: ::: {#29098e28 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(5) # path: 1-2-3-4-5 edge_ids = graph.get_edge_ids()[1:3] graph.select_edges_by_id(edge_ids) graph.delete_edges_ws() graph.count_nodes(), graph.count_edges() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (5, 2) ``` ::: ::: The path is now split into three pieces, with node "3" left isolated: ::: {#79929609 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.count_weakly_connected_components(), graph.get_degree("3") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (3, 0) ``` ::: ::: Selecting edges by predicate makes it easy to prune a graph based on edge attributes, such as removing low-weight connections: ::: {#94d63b8f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges([("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 5.0), ("C", "D", 2.0)]) ) graph.select_edges(lambda e: e.weight is not None and e.weight < 2.0) graph.delete_edges_ws() # only the two edges with weight >= 2.0 remain graph.get_edge_df() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ```{=html}
